objective: T-20260930-03: test on local US daily data whether year-to-date losers (ADV top 1,500, price >= 5 USD, funds excluded) bought at the open after 15 December and held to 15 or 31 January beat the equal-weight pool after ADV-tiered costs (3/6/12 bp per side) in ten December windows 2016-2025. Registry direction dir:tax_loss_selling_year_end_rebound; six preregistered candidates.
target_regime_and_horizon: Seasonal window 16 December to 15/31 January, ten annual observations 2016-2025 plus February and June placebo windows and a 15 November diagnostic window; long-only equal-weight baskets of about 150 stocks (100 in the 501-1,500 pool), two trades a year. A pass would only license a forward-only tracking task with not_before 2026-12-15 (the true out-of-sample window); no paper trading.
existing_solution_comparison: Published: Ivkovic-Poterba-Weisbenner (NBER w10275) and Grinblatt-Keloharju show tax-loss selling and turn-of-the-year buying pressure in trade data; Schwert (w9277) shows the small-minus-large first-two-weeks-of-January spread through 2001; Kaul et al. (2025) find January returns larger for capital-loss, illiquid and volatile stocks over 1874-1917; McLean-Pontiff estimate about 35% post-publication decay. Practitioner packaging (Quantpedia) is a small-cap tilt with numbers ending 2007; a Globe and Mail summary of a TSX loser rebound and a JFIR 'fading' snippet were not readable (claim_only). No opened source gives a US year-to-date-loser price effect after 2015, so nothing can be reused as an effect size; the local test is the only missing evidence and it is nearly free.
remaining_evidence_gap: The size, after 2016 and after tiered costs, of the mid-December to January excess return of US year-to-date losers versus the equal-weight pool in liquid stocks, and whether it separates from the same construction in February-March and June-July.
negative_experiments_checked: oc research directions check tax loss (2026-09-30): dir:tax_loss_selling_year_end_rebound is queued (no prior verdict); other hits are unrelated (collective2 extreme-os, ema_crossover, meta-strategy rotation, momentum risk control). grep -ril 'tax.loss|january effect' over reports/research/control, iterations, ledger finds only queue/intel text and source snapshots for other iterations (sector seasonality papers), no prior local experiment of this signal. Related closed directions are different mechanisms (end-of-month reversal, sector seasonality).
cost_and_execution_assumptions: Per-side cost by ADV rank on the signal day: 1-500 3 bp, 501-1000 6 bp, 1001-1500 12 bp (SPREAD_BPS_TIERS, scripts/run_h20260929_21_lockup_books.py), round trip 2x; entry at the daily-bar open after the signal close, exit at the close; no borrow (long only); benchmark equal-weight pool without costs (conservative), IWM-hedged version reported separately. Signal close -> next open fill as in the frozen protocol; sanitize_price_matrices defaults plus a split-like session filter on the window.

cheapest_decisive_test.action: Run scripts/run_h20260930_03_tax_loss_year_end.py: ten annual excess tables for six candidates, net mean, year-clustered t, positive years, mean without best year, Dec 2024 and Dec 2025, February and June placebo means, W1 diagnostic, IWM-hedged version.
cheapest_decisive_test.pass_condition: For a candidate: mean net excess >= +1.5%, >= 7 of 10 years positive, year-clustered t >= 2.0, placebo means summing to at most half of the real mean, and both Dec 2024 and Dec 2025 positive.
cheapest_decisive_test.falsification_condition: Any of the five conditions failing for every candidate closes the direction as refuted (tax-loss rebound closed); no ledger, no threshold change.

stop_condition: Frozen before any result: close as refuted if no candidate meets all five continue conditions in hypotheses.md; a pass is only a forward-only watch item with not_before 2026-12-15. No change to pool, thresholds, exits, cost tiers, windows or candidates after seeing results.

sources.claim: Ivkovic, Poterba and Weisbenner (NBER w10275, January 2004) compare a large discount broker's individual-investor trades in taxable versus tax-deferred accounts and find tax-loss selling throughout the calendar year, most pronounced in December and especially for investors who realized capital gains elsewhere in the portfolio, plus a capital-gains lock-in effect.
sources.market_and_period: US discount-broker individual accounts, 1990s trade data
sources.applicability: Establishes that December selling of losers by taxable individuals exists; motivates the mid-December entry.
sources.limitations: Trade-level evidence only; gives no stock-price return size for a December-to-January rebound, and covers the 1990s before the growth of tax-sheltered accounts.
sources.independent_replication: Corroborated by Grinblatt and Keloharju (Finland, same tax-loss pattern); no US post-2015 replication opened.

sources.claim: Grinblatt and Keloharju (draft 2002-07-03, NBER w8745) find that Finnish investors realize losses more than gains toward the end of December and repurchase the sold stocks, producing net tax-loss buying pressure that is negative before the turn of the year and positive afterwards, and that turn-of-the-year returns, particularly for small firms, relate to that pressure.
sources.market_and_period: Finnish stocks, household and institutional trades, 1990s
sources.applicability: Supports the sign of the price pressure (December negative, January positive) that the mid-December entry tries to harvest.
sources.limitations: Finnish market with a different tax regime; 1990s sample; regression evidence, no tradeable long-only excess return net of costs.
sources.independent_replication: Same direction as Ivkovic-Poterba-Weisbenner for US individuals; Kaul et al. 2025 find the effect also existed in 1874-1917 without income taxes.

sources.claim: Schwert (NBER w9277) shows on CRSP data that the small-minus-large NYSE return difference in the first 15 calendar days of January was still reliably positive after publication (daily alpha 0.00641, t 9.87, 1962-2001; 0.00565, t 5.37, 1990-2001), while the small-firm premium overall was much smaller after 1982 than in 1926-1982.
sources.applicability: Shows the turn-of-the-year window effect survived publication through 2001 for the small-minus-large spread; ends 2001, so it says nothing about 2016-2026.
sources.limitations: Size spread, not year-to-date losers; ends in 2001; the fading after 2001 is not measured.
sources.independent_replication: Keim (1983) and Reinganum (1983) are the original results; the JFIR 'revisited' paper reportedly finds fading later (claim_only).

sources.claim: Kaul, Mehrotra, Morck and Phillips (EFMA 2025 working paper) document a 3.1 percent January price increase in NYSE stocks over 1874-1917, before income taxes, and find larger January returns for small stocks, stocks with capital losses, illiquid stocks and volatile stocks, pointing to arbitrage costs as the reason the effect persists.
sources.applicability: Supports that losers and illiquid stocks carry the larger January return, and argues against pure tax explanation; so the pool restriction to ADV top 1,500 may remove the illiquid stocks where the effect is largest.
sources.limitations: Historic sample before income taxes and modern institutions; not a 2016-2026 estimate; working-paper draft.
sources.independent_replication: Consistent with Roll (1983) as cited by the authors; no independent replication opened.

sources.claim: McLean and Pontiff (October 2012 working-paper version of the JF 2016 article) study 82 published return predictors and find that the average post-publication decay, attributed to both statistical bias and price pressure from aware investors, is about 35 percent, larger for anomaly portfolios of large, liquid stocks.
sources.market_and_period: 82 US stock characteristics, publication-date splits, up to 2011
sources.applicability: Prior that a 1983-era calendar anomaly is weaker in 2016-2025 and weaker in liquid stocks; sets the low prior stated in the queue.
sources.limitations: Average across 82 characteristics; the January-loser effect is not singled out.
sources.independent_replication: Published version JF 2016; used elsewhere in this repository.

sources.claim: Anderson, Gerlach and DiTraglia (William and Mary WP 15, March 2005) find in two laboratory auction environments that prices in the January markets were systematically higher than those in December, suggesting a psychological contribution to the January effect.
sources.applicability: Weak side evidence that a January-over-December price gap can arise without taxes.
sources.limitations: Lab experiment; no market data; no return size for a stock strategy.
